NOTE 102

Form 289 (If $S$ is a set of subsets of a countable set and $S$ is closed under chain unions, then $S$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element.) is false in $\mathcal{M}1$. Let $b$ be the generic set of generic reals in $\mathcal{M}1$, let $E(b)$ be the set of all finite subsets of $b$, and let $S=\{\cup x:x\in E(b)\}$. Since $b$ is generic, for any finite subset $\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}$ of $b,\,a_{0}\not \subseteq \cup \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}$ It follows that if $x,\,y\in E(b)$, then $\cup x\subseteq \cup y$ iff $x\subseteq y$. Hence, any chain in $S$ corresponds to a chain in $E(b)$ and a $\subseteq$-maximal element of $S$ corresponds to a $\subseteq$-maximal element of $E(b)$. We claim that there is no infinite chain in $E(b)$. For suppose $x_{0}\subset x_{1}\subset x_{2}\cdots$ is an infinite chain in $E(b)$. Let $a_{n}$ be the smallest element in $x_{n+1}-x_{n}$ for $n\in \omega$. Then $\{a_{n}:n\in \omega \}$ is a denumerable subset of $b$, which is impossible because $b$ is Dedekind finite. Thus, all chains in $E(b)$ are finite so $E(b)$ is closed under chain unions. Consequently, $S$ is closed under chain unions. Since $b$ is infinite, $E(b)$ has no $\subseteq$-maximal element and, therefore, $S$ has no $\subseteq$-maximal element.

NOTE 104

If $N=N(A,\,\mathcal{G},\,S)$ is a permutation model, then the $2m=m$ principle (form 3) is false in $N$ if the following holds in $N$:

$$\begin{equation*} \begin{split} (\forall E\in S)&[A-E\neq \emptyset \\ &\wedge (\forall a\in A-E)(\forall b\in A-\{a\})(\exists \sigma \in \mathcal{G})(\forall c\in E)(\sigma (c)=c\\ &\wedge (\sigma (a)\neq a\wedge \sigma (b)=b)\\ &\vee (\sigma (a)=b\wedge \sigma (b)=a\wedge (\forall c\in A-\{a,\,b\})\sigma (c)=c))]. \end{split} \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}$$

Examples of models that satisfy $(\ast )$ are $\mathcal{N}1,\,\mathcal{N}2,\,\mathcal{N}2(\aleph _{\alpha })$, and $\mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{\alpha })$.

NOTE 106

This note contains results from McCarten [1988] and Schnare [1968] relating to forms [1 BF] (D$T_{0})$, [1 BG] (C$T_{0})$, [1 BH] (T$T_{0})$, and [1 BI] (M$T_{0})$.

[1 BF] (D$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is dense in $X$. ($Y$ is dense in $X$ if there is no non-empty open subset $O\subseteq X$ such that $O\cap Y=\emptyset .)$

[1 BG] (C$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is codense in $X$. ($Y$ is codense in $X$ if there is no non-empty closed subset $C\subseteq X$ such that $C\cap Y=\emptyset .)$

[1 BH] (T$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is thick in $X$. $(Y$ is thick in $X$ if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset $H\subseteq X$ such that $H\cap Y=\emptyset$.)

[1 BI] (M$T_{0}$): Every topological space has a maximal $T_{0}$ subspace.

1.

Forms $\mathrm{D}T_{0}$ and $\mathrm{C}T_{0}$ are false if “$T_{0}$” is replaced by “$T_{1}$”. (A counter example is the topological space $(\mathbb{R},\,\tau )$, where $\tau =\{G\subseteq \mathbb{R}:G=(a,\,\infty )$, $a\in \mathbb{R} \vee G= \emptyset \vee G=\mathbb{R}\}.)$ McCarten [1988].

2.

Form $\mathrm{T}T_{0}$ remains equivalent to $\mathrm{AC}$ if $T_{0}$ is replaced by $T_{n}$, for any $n$ such that $T_{n}$ implies $T_{0}$. McCarten [1988].

3.

$\mathrm{M}T_{0}$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{M}T_{1}$. Schnare [1968].

4.

Schnare [1968] shows that the statement $\mathrm{MP}$ is false if $\mathrm{P}=T_{2},\,T_{3},\,T_{4}$, regular, completely regular, normal, paracompact, metrizable, linearly disconnected or discrete. (It follows from the lemma that if P is a property that is possessed by every finite discrete space, but not by a countably infinite minimal $T_{1}$ space, then MP is false.)

NOTE 107

Good/Tree [1995] proves that each of [34 B] through [34 E] implies 34. In this note we supply the details of the converses.

In Kelley [1955], pages 173–2 there is an outline of a proof that form [34 B] ($\omega _{1}$ with the order topology is not paracompact.) follows from $\mathrm{AC}$. We note that the proof requires only form 34 ($\omega _{1}$ is regular.) and therefore 34 implies [34 B].

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the open cover of $\omega _{1}$ from Kelley’s hint. That is, $\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1}\}$. We show that $\mathcal{C}$ has no open, locally finite refinement by contradiction. Assume that $\mathcal{A}$ is an open, locally finite refinement of $\mathcal{C}$. We define an increasing function $f:\omega \rightarrow \omega _{1}$ by induction: $f(0)=0$. Assume that $f(n)$ is defined. For each $\beta \leq f(n)$, the set $D_{\beta }=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:\beta \in x\}$ is finite since $\mathcal{A}$ is locally finite. It’s also true that for each $x\in D_{\beta },\, \sup \{\gamma :\gamma \in x\}$ is less that $\omega _{1}$ since $x$ is a subset of one of the elements of $\mathcal{C}$. Let $g(\beta )$ be the maximum of $\{\sup (x):x\in D_{\beta }\}$. $g(\beta )$ is also less than $\omega _{1}$. Now apply form 34 to the set $W=\{g(\beta ):\beta \leq f(n)\}$. This is a countable set of ordinals each $<\omega _{1}$ and therefore $\sup W<\omega _{1}$. Let $f(n+1)$ be the least ordinal greater than $\sup W$. The important property of the function $f$ is that

$$\begin{equation*} (\forall n\in \omega )(\forall j<n)(\forall x\in \mathcal{A})(f(j)\in x\rightarrow f(n)\not \in x) \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}$$

The sequence $\langle f(n)\rangle _{n\in \omega }$ is strictly increasing so its $\sup$ (call the $\sup \, \beta$) is a limit ordinal. Further, by form 34, $\beta <\omega _{1}$. Since $\mathcal{A}$ is locally finite, there is an (open) neighborhood $y$ of $\beta$ such that $\{x\in \mathcal{A}:x\cap \,y\neq \emptyset \}$ is finite. Since $y$ is open and $\beta$ is a limit ordinal, there is an ordinal $\gamma <\beta$ such that the interval $(\gamma ,\,\beta +1)\subseteq y$. For some natural number $k$, this interval must contain $f(n)$ for all $n\geq k$. For each $n\geq k$ we consider the sets $D_{f(n)}=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:f(n)\in x\}$. These sets are pairwise disjoint (by $(\ast )$), each is non-empty and for each element $x\in D_{f(n)},\, x\cap (\gamma ,\, \beta +1)\neq \emptyset$. Therefore $\{x\in \mathcal{C}:x\cap \,y\neq \emptyset \}$ is infinite, a contradiction.

To show that 34 implies [34 C] $(\omega _{1}$ with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in $\omega _{1}$.), let $X$ be an infinite subset of $\omega _{1}$. Since $X$ is well ordered and infinite, it must have an initial segment of order type $\omega$. Form 34 implies that each such initial segment must be bounded, so the least upper bound of this set is a limit point of $X$ in $\omega _{1}$.

If $\omega _{1}$ is regular and contains a denumerable discrete family of open sets, then the set of smallest elements in each set would be an infinite set with no limit point, contradicting [34 C]. Thus, 34 implies [34 D] $(\omega _{1}$ with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets.).

The uncountable open cover of $\omega ,\,\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1} \}$, described above does not contain a countable subcover. If it did we could construct a countable cofinal sequence in $\omega _{1}$, contradicting 34. Therefore, 34 implies [34 E] $(\omega _{1}$ with the order topology is not Lindelöf.).

NOTE 108

We give the proof that each pair of cardinal numbers has a greatest lower bound (glb) (form 187) is true in $\mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{1})$. (The proof is due to A. Rubin.)

Finally, if $X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\alpha _{q}\times q$ and $Y \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\beta _{q}\times q$ are the representations of $X$ and $Y$, we claim that $Z= \bigcup _{q\in Q}\min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q})\,\times \, q$ has the property that $|Z|= \mathrm{glb}(|X|,\,|Y|)$. Clearly, $|Z|\leq |X|$ and $|Z|\leq |Y|$. Suppose, $|Z_{0}|\leq |X|$ and $|Z_{0}|\leq |Y|$. Also, suppose $Z_{0} \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\gamma _{q}\times q$ is the representation of $Z_{0}$. By the lemma, $\gamma _{q}\leq \alpha _{q}$ and $\gamma _{q}\leq \beta _{q}$ for all $q$. Thus, $\gamma _{q}\leq \min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q})$ for all $q$ so it follows that $|Z_{0}|\leq |Z|$.

NOTE 110

In this note we prove the result from G. Moore [1982] that form 36 (If $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $A \bigcap B$ is countable for every bounded $B$ then $A$ is countable.) implies form 38 ($\mathbb{R}$ is not the union of a countable family of countable sets.)

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that form 38 is false and therefore that $\mathbb{R} = \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}$ where each $A_{n}$ is countable. Let $f$ be any bijection between $\mathbb{R}$ and the interval $(0,1)$. For each $n\in \omega$ let $A_{n}^{\prime }=f^{\prime \prime }A_{n}+n$ (where for any set $X$ of reals and any real $t,\,X+t=\{x+t:x\in X\})$. Then

(a)

$A_{n}^{\prime }\subseteq (n,\,n+1)$

(b)

$|A_{n}^{\prime }|=|A_{n}|$ and therefore each $A_{n}$ is countable.

(c)

There is an injection from $\mathbb{R}= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}$ to $\bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }(x\mapsto f(x)+n$ where $n$ is the least natural number such that $x\in A_{n}$).

Let $A= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }$. It follows from (a) that every bounded subset of $A$ is contained in some finite union $\bigcup _{n<N}A_{n}^{\prime }$. Hence, by (b), every bounded subset of $A$ is countable. By (c), $A$ is uncountable hence form 36 is false.

The relationships between the forms $336(n)$ and $342(n)$ were discussed by C. Montenegro in a talk at the Latin American Logic Symposium in Bogota, 1995. $(336(n)$ is: If $X$ is infinite then there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ such that $\{t\subseteq Y:|t|=n\}$ has a choice function and $342(n)$ is $PC(\infty ,\,n,\, \infty ).)$ He noted that for $n=2$ or 3, $336(n)$ clearly implies $342(n)$. NOTE 112

In this note we prove that in $\mathcal{N}41$, form 9 (Dedekind finite and finite are equivalent) is true and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0}))$ is true.

It will follow from the lemma below that form 9 $(DF=F)$ and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0}))$ are true in $\mathcal{N}41$.

To show that $C(WO,\,<\aleph _{0})$ is true in $\mathcal{N}41$ let $Y$ be a well ordered set of finite sets in $\mathcal{N}41$. Suppose that $E$ is a support of a well ordering of $Y$. Then for each $x$ in $Y,\,E$ is a support of $x$. By the lemma, since $x$ is finite, $E$ is a support of every element of $x$. It follows that if $f$ is any choice function for $Y$ (in the ground model) then $E$ is a support of $f$.

NOTE 116

A proof that form 304 (There does not exist a $T_{2}$ topological space $X$ such that every infinite subset of $X$ contains an infinite compact subset.) is true in $\mathcal{N}1$.

Let $X$ be an infinite $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ topological space in $\mathcal{N}1$. We need to show that there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X\ (Y\in \mathcal{N}1)$ such that $Y$ has no infinite compact subsets (in $\mathcal{N}1)$. If $X$ is well orderable then it is clear that such a $Y$ exists. Assume that $X$ is not well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$.

Choose an $x\in X$, a support $E$, an element $a\in A$, and a permutation $\phi \in G$ which fixes $E$ pointwise so that

(a)

$E$ is a support of $X$ and its topology.

(b)

$E\cup \{a\}$ is a support of $x$ and

(c)

$\phi (x)\neq x$. (And therefore by (b) $\phi (a)\neq a$.)

By the lemma, the set of pairs $F=\{(\psi (x),\,\psi (a)):\psi \in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise} is a one to one function (in the model $\mathcal{N}1$) from $Y=_{\mathrm{def}}\{\psi (x):\psi \in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise} onto $A-E$.

Since the topology on $X$ is $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ we can choose open sets $C$ and $D$ so that $x\in C,\,\phi (x)\in D$ and $C\cap D=\emptyset$. Since $Y$ can be put in a one to one correspondence with a subset of the atoms in the model, every subset of $Y$ in the model must be finite or cofinite. This means that at least one of $Y\cap C$ or $Y\cap D$ is finite. We may assume that $Y\cap C$ is finite by replacing $C$ by $C\cap \phi ^{-1}(D)$ if necessary. Under this assumption we can conclude that $\mathcal{C}=\{\psi (C):\psi \in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise} is an open cover for $Y$. Further each element of $\mathcal{C}$ is finite. It follows that for any infinite subset $Z$ of $Y,\,\mathcal{C}$ is an open cover for $Z$ without a finite subcover.
